notes: Recent-complaint misdirection in word-against-word rape trial; conviction quashed with retrial ordered.

enrichment.short_title: Gill: unsafe conviction for failure to direct on recent complaint
key_facts: Leslie John Gill was convicted at Portsmouth Crown Court of rape after a night at Tony Featherstone's flat and sentenced to six years' imprisonment.

The prosecution case was that the complainant woke to find Gill having sexual intercourse with her without consent; Gill said there was no penetration and she had consented to kissing and partial undressing.
The sole ground of appeal was that the judge failed to give a specific direction on recent complaint evidence, including texts to Tracey and Jodie.
The case turned entirely on credibility with no forensic support for penetration; medical evidence was inconclusive.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction by limited leave of the single judge on the recent-complaint direction ground.
enrichment.outcome: The conviction was quashed as unsafe because of the misdirection, but a retrial was ordered in the public interest; Gill was granted bail pending rearraignment.
enrichment.ratio: Where recent complaint evidence is admitted in a word-against-word sexual offence trial, the judge must direct the jury that it is not independent evidence of truth but may assist credibility assessment; failure to do so can render a conviction unsafe even if counsel did not invite the direction.
legal_issues: Whether the judge was required to give a Judicial Studies Board direction on recent complaint
Whether recent complaint here was so immediate as to need no special direction
Whether the conviction was nevertheless safe despite the absence of direction
Whether a retrial should be ordered
linked_authorities: R v Islam [1999] 1 Cr App R 22
R v S [2004] EWCA Crim 1320

confidence.notes: Single ground of appeal, clear misdirection finding and retrial order.

notes: EIA screening at reserved matters stage; collateral challenge to earlier outline permissions rejected.

enrichment.short_title: Noble Organisation v Thanet: EIA at reserved matters approval

statutes_considered.title: Town and Country Planning (Environmental Impact Assessment) Regulations 1999

key_facts: The claimant challenged Thanet's May 2004 reserved matters approval for leisure development at EuroKent Business Park, Ramsgate, arguing EIA should have been required.
Outline permissions for a business park (1997) and leisure uses (2002) had not been challenged and earlier screening decisions rejected EIA.
The council considered EIA again at reserved matters stage amid uncertainty following Wells and the Barker ECJ reference.
The claimant contended the council unlawfully benchmarked against earlier permissions whose EIA treatment was itself defective.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed permission application treated as substantive judicial review after permission granted at the hearing.
enrichment.outcome: The claim was dismissed; earlier unchallenged outline permissions and screening decisions were valid material considerations and the reserved matters EIA decision was lawful.
enrichment.ratio: Unchallenged planning permissions and EIA screening decisions must be treated as valid and cannot be collaterally impugned in later proceedings; where EIA is reconsidered at reserved matters, comparison with the extant outline permission is permissible and Wells does not require treating earlier decisions as invalid.
legal_issues: Whether EIA could lawfully be considered at the reserved matters stage
Whether reliance on earlier outline permissions involved an indirect challenge to their lawfulness
Whether comparison with the business park permission rendered the screening decision irrational
Whether Wells required nullification of earlier EIA failures

notes: Esso licensee group litigation on BPR margin adjustments and hot fuel measurement; appeal dismissed.

enrichment.short_title: Addison v Esso: licence margin adjustments and hot fuel

statutes_considered.title: Weights and Measures (Liquid Fuel Carried by Road Tanker) Order 1985

key_facts: About 100 Esso retail licensees appealed Moore-Bick J's construction of standard partnership licence agreements governing margins, fees and operating cost allowances.
Esso introduced Business Process Redesign in 1995-1996, adjusting financial terms after benchmarking costs against the most efficient 25% of licensees.
Licensees argued reviews were not contractually permitted and adjustments were arbitrary; they also claimed short delivery where fuel was measured hot at terminal loading.
The court rejected new construction arguments not run at trial and upheld rationality findings on BPR implementation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Commercial Court group litigation judgment on generic contractual construction and breach issues.
enrichment.outcome: The appeal was dismissed; Clause 6 gave Esso broad discretion subject to irrationality limits, and fuel was sold on established industry practice of observed volume at loading.
enrichment.ratio: Clause 6 of Esso's licence agreements permitted Esso to adjust margins and allowances after review by reference to wider commercial circumstances, not merely site-specific operating costs; hot fuel measured at terminal loading did not breach contract where industry practice did not require standard-litre accounting.
legal_issues: Whether annual review under Clause 6 was limited to site-specific competent licensee costs
Whether 'necessary' adjustments required objective justification
Whether BPR adjustments were arbitrary, capricious or irrational
Whether fuel volume should be measured at ambient or standard temperature
linked_authorities: Addison & Ors v Esso Petroleum Co Ltd [2003] EWHC 1730 (Comm)
Horkulak v Cantor Fitzgerald International [2004] EWCA Civ 1287

notes: Late pre-emptive costs cap application in telecom mast Code objection claim refused.

enrichment.short_title: Petursson v Hutchison 3G: pre-emptive costs cap refused
key_facts: Claimants sought relocation of Hutchison 3G apparatus near Worcester under paragraph 17 of the Electronic Communications Code after alleging health effects.
The defendant estimated total costs of about £233,000 while claimants estimated under £30,000; claimants later abandoned damages claims.
Claimants applied in October 2004 to cap the defendant's recoverable profit costs at £20,000, having known of the estimate since February.
The defendant said about £194,000 had already been incurred and a three-day trial was listed for February 2005.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for pre-emptive costs capping order shortly before trial in transferred Technology and Construction Court proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Both retrospective and prospective costs cap applications were refused; costs budgeting at this late stage was inappropriate and proportionality should be addressed on detailed assessment.
enrichment.ratio: Costs cap orders should normally be prospective and made at an early stage; a late retrospective cap after substantial compliant expenditure by the paying party would breach fairness, and the Smart test for caps was not satisfied on these facts.
legal_issues: Whether the court could impose a retrospective costs cap
Whether a prospective cap was needed to prevent disproportionate future costs
Whether Article 6 required a cap given claimants' means
Whether defendant's estimated hours and City rates were disproportionate

notes: Parole Board recall upheld where known mental illness manifested dangerously after release.

enrichment.short_title: Irving v Parole Board: recall for known mental disorder risk
key_facts: Mr Irving was sentenced in 1998 to eight years for robbery and indecent assault and automatically released on licence in June 2003.
After release to a probation hostel he displayed escalating paranoid behaviour toward staff, leading to a July 2003 recall recommendation.
Psychiatric evidence before sentence had identified paranoid ideation and serious danger, especially to women.
The Parole Board rejected representations against recall in November 2004, finding unacceptable risk despite the disorder being known pre-release.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of Parole Board deferral decision treated as challenge to the November 2004 recall confirmation.
enrichment.outcome: The application failed; recall was lawful because the Board assessed current unacceptable risk, not whether risk had increased since release.
enrichment.ratio: On representations against recall the Parole Board must ask whether the prisoner's liberty presents an unacceptable risk of further offending, not whether risk exceeds that at automatic release; known mental illness can justify recall if post-release conduct creates a new quantified risk.
legal_issues: Whether recall required proof that risk had increased since release
Whether known pre-release mental disorder prevented lawful recall
Whether refusal of an oral hearing was flawed
Whether Articles 5 and 14 ECHR were engaged

linked_authorities: R v Smith v Parole Board [2003] EWCA Civ 1269
R (Clift) v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2004] 1 WLR 2223

notes: CCRC reference on section 34 silence direction after Beckles v UK; convictions quashed with retrial.

enrichment.short_title: Beckles: section 34 misdirection on legal advice to remain silent

statutes_considered.title: Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994

key_facts: Keith Beckles was convicted in 1997 of robbery, false imprisonment and attempted murder after Mohammed Abdi was robbed and thrown from a Hackney flat, suffering permanent paraplegia.
At first police interview Beckles answered 'no comment' on solicitor's advice despite earlier spontaneous remarks that the victim had jumped.
The ECtHR held in Beckles v UK that the section 34 direction violated Article 6 because the jury were not properly directed on reliance on legal advice.
The CCRC referred the case; the Court of Appeal found a misdirection and quashed convictions but ordered retrial.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Reference by the Criminal Cases Review Commission under section 9 of the 1995 Act following ECtHR violation finding.
enrichment.outcome: Convictions were quashed as unsafe because the jury were not directed on genuineness and reasonableness of reliance on legal advice; a retrial was ordered.
enrichment.ratio: Where a defendant relies on legal advice to remain silent under section 34, the jury must be directed to consider whether he genuinely and reasonably relied on that advice and whether silence truly explained failure to mention trial facts; a section 34 direction may be inappropriate where the defence was not an ambush.
legal_issues: Whether the trial judge misdirected on section 34 inferences
Whether ECtHR standards applied despite pre-HRA trial
Whether a section 34 direction should have been given at all
Whether convictions were safe notwithstanding Mohamoud's identification evidence
linked_authorities: Beckles v United Kingdom (2003) 36 EHRR 13
R v Webber [2004] 1 WLR 404
R v Hoare and Pierce [2004] EWCA Crim 784

confidence.notes: Five-judge court with detailed section 34 analysis and clear quashing/retrial order.

notes: VAT article 4.5 direct effect for local authority off-street parking; Marleasing rewrite rejected.

enrichment.short_title: Customs v Isle of Wight: VAT article 4.5 direct effect
key_facts: Isle of Wight Council claimed repayment of VAT on off-street parking under section 80 VATA, arguing public authority exemption under article 4.5 of the Sixth Directive.
The tribunal held the council's parking was within the special legal regime of article 4.5(1) but that the competition limb in article 4.5(2) was not properly implemented in UK law.
Customs appealed the implementation issue, contending VATA could be read compatibly via Marleasing or that article 4.5 was directly effective in full.
Pumfrey J held the whole of article 4.5 was directly applicable between the council and Customs, remitting competition assessment to the tribunal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court appeal from VAT and Duties Tribunal preliminary issues decision.
enrichment.outcome: Customs' appeal was allowed; article 4.5(1) and (2) are directly effective and the tribunal must assess whether non-taxation would cause significant competition distortion.
enrichment.ratio: Where UK VAT law treats all local authority taxable supplies as chargeable without the article 4.5 public-authority/competition structure, Marleasing cannot wholesale rewrite the charging regime, but a public body may rely directly on both subparagraphs of article 4.5 against the tax authority.
legal_issues: Whether article 4.5(2) was properly implemented in VATA
Whether Marleasing could read article 4.5 into the definition of business
Whether article 4.5(2) was too uncertain for direct effect
Whether a council could rely on article 4.5(1) without accepting article 4.5(2)

Case C-106/89 Marleasing SA v La Comercial Internacional de Alimentacion SA
Institute of Chartered Accountants v Customs and Excise [1996] STC 799

notes: Harmondsworth fast-track asylum system held not inherently unfair; written flexibility policy required.

enrichment.short_title: Refugee Legal Centre v SSHD: Harmondsworth fast track fairness
key_facts: The Refugee Legal Centre challenged the lawfulness of the Harmondsworth fast-track asylum process for single male claimants from 'whitelist' countries.
The scheme compressed instructions, asylum interview and decision into roughly three days, with appeal stages following in quick succession.
Statistics showed very high refusal rates but some successes on appeal; RLC did not participate in the scheme.
The Court of Appeal agreed with Collins J that the system was not inherently unfair but lacked a published flexibility policy.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Expedited appeal from Administrative Court refusal of declaration that Harmondsworth fast track was unlawful.
enrichment.outcome: The appeal failed; the system is lawful if operated flexibly, but officials need a written policy identifying when the standard timetable must be enlarged.
enrichment.ratio: An asylum fast-track is not inherently unfair merely because it is compressed, but fairness requires a clear published policy for extending the timetable where vulnerability, exhaustion or need for post-interview representations demands it; built-in appeals do not cure unfair initial interviews.
legal_issues: Whether Harmondsworth fast track carried unacceptable risk of unfairness
Whether same-day legal advice and asylum interview was inherently unfair
Whether appellate safeguards cured initial procedural defects
Whether relief should follow R (Q) v Home Secretary

notes: Mobile agricultural sheds on wheels held not buildings; section 187B injunction largely agreed.

enrichment.short_title: Tewkesbury v Keeley: mobile sheds not planning development

statutes_considered.title: Caravan Sites and Control of Development Act 1960

key_facts: Tewkesbury Borough Council sought a section 187B injunction against Michael Keeley over long-running unauthorised uses at Warren Farm near Toddington.
Keeley manufactured timber structures on steel chassis with wheels, assembled on site for alleged agricultural use including chicken housing.
Earlier wooden buildings had failed appeal against enforcement notices; Keeley then developed towable 'mobile sheds'.
Most injunction terms were agreed; dispute centred on whether assembled and unassembled sheds required planning permission.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial of planning injunction claim with agreed permanent order save for status of mobile sheds.
enrichment.outcome: A section 187B injunction was granted in agreed terms; the assembled mobile shed was not a building so on-site assembly was not operational development, but unassembled chassis storage was material change of use.
enrichment.ratio: A towable agricultural shed resting on wheels and breeze blocks, substantially prefabricated off site and freely movable, is not a 'building' for planning purposes; placing caravans or analogous mobile structures does not constitute a building operation though change of use may still arise.
legal_issues: Whether section 187B should be exercised given enforcement history
Whether on-site assembly of mobile sheds was building operations
Whether the structure was a building applying size, permanence and attachment tests
Whether storing unassembled chassis on land was material change of use

notes: Section 75 applies to four-party card transactions but not foreign supply contracts.

enrichment.short_title: OFT v Lloyds TSB: section 75 four-party and overseas cards
key_facts: The OFT sought declarations on connected lender liability under section 75 for Visa, MasterCard and American Express credit card transactions.
Card issuers argued four-party network transactions lacked arrangements between creditor and supplier and that overseas purchases fell outside the section.
Representative proceedings involved Lloyds TSB, Tesco Personal Finance and American Express Services Europe.
Industry practice had long disputed overseas and four-party scope despite voluntary ex gratia handling in some cases.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Commercial Court representative declaratory action on construction of section 75 for UK card issuers.
enrichment.outcome: Section 75 applies to four-party domestic transactions but not where the supply contract was made abroad, governed by foreign law and performed abroad; section 187(3) did not exclude four-party arrangements.
enrichment.ratio: Credit card agreements finance supplier transactions and network rules create 'arrangements between' issuers and merchants even without direct contracts, engaging section 75; however, absent express extra-territorial wording, section 75 does not impose like liability for foreign supply contracts not governed by UK law or amenable to UK jurisdiction.
legal_issues: Whether four-party transactions are restricted-use credit agreements financing supplier transactions
Whether arrangements exist between card issuer and supplier under section 12(b)
Whether section 187(3) disregards those arrangements
Whether section 75 applies to overseas credit card purchases

Re British Slag Ltd's Application [1963] 1 WLR 727
Clark v Oceanic Contractors Inc [1983] 2 AC 130
